newsitem.title: USA: US FCC chief criticizes spectrum legislation.
newsitem.headline: US FCC chief criticizes spectrum legislation.

text.p: The head of the Federal Communications Commission Wednesday criticized congressional legislation covering U.S. airwave auctions, saying it would hurt efforts to give more spectrum to public-safety officials and communications firms.
The legislation is meant to implement the recent budget accord between President Clinton and Congress.

FCC Chairman Reed Hundt said the House bill would reverse his agency's decision to provide public safety and commercial users with new channels recovered from television broadcasters, following the transition to digital TV.
Broadcasters are supposed to return their existing analog spectrum to the government by the year 2006, under new FCC rules.
The spectrum is supposed to be auctioned in the year 2001 for other uses as well as provide public-safety officials with more airwave space.

Hundt, in a speech to the Citizens for a Sound Economy, also said the House and Senate legislation could convert what was to be a loan of new digital TV licenses into a permanent gift by undercutting broadcaters' obligations to use the licenses and to return their analog licenses.

The FCC chairman also said the House measure could effectively eliminate the FCC's ability to hold auctions. He asserted that imposing minimum bid requirements threatens to undermine auctions by creating uncertainty that would inhibit auction participation and impede capital formation.
